items.finding: None as worded. But the brief asks for both directions where the source has both, and this source has both for THC. The fall in femoral blood between repeated post-mortem samples (one study, ref 30) sits beside a statement that THC in femoral blood after death was higher than in samples from life (refs 30, 42; p. 6). The review also reports rabbit heart-blood THC rising by 2 h after death while lung THC fell (ref 32; p. 5). Saying both ('fell between repeated samples after death, but was higher after death than in samples from life') would match the source and strengthen 'hard to read'.
items.reason: Own full Borra PDF read and numerical page rendered: retain THC fall in repeated post-mortem sampling and higher post-mortem than ante-mortem THC as separate, second-hand comparisons. New extraction carries both and timing/matrix/absorption limitations.

items.finding: The facts check, but three paraphrases run slightly stronger than the source. (1) The heart-to-femoral ratio: the review says a ratio different from 1 suggests redistribution only if central and femoral levels were equal at death, says it is no marker of extent, and adds that a ratio of 1 does not exclude redistribution. 'Shows that change after death occurred' should read 'can indicate', and the ratio-of-1 point should be added. (2) 'Concludes that the size of the change cannot yet be tied to drug properties or to features of the case': the review says evidence linking redistribution to specific variables is often lacking. It says drug properties are 'only part of the toxicological puzzle', with general consensus that some properties contribute (e.g. basic drugs), and calls case features underexplored but promising, citing significant C/P differences by BMI, decomposition state and other variables. 'Can so far be tied only partly to drug properties, and features of the case are little studied' is closer. (3) The 17 h mean covers only studies where the interval was available or estimated (12 references, 7 of them outside Tables 1-2, including reports of one and two cases, refs 76-77). 'Does not appraise the studies' is fair: there is no study-level appraisal. Designs are ranked A/B/C by expected contribution, and Fig. 1 lists quality among reasons for excluding 17 publications, without criteria.
items.reason: Full Borra source and rendered §§5–6: can indicate conditional on equal concentrations in life, ratio 1 does not exclude change, timing mean only available/estimated intervals, and case-variable links are not entirely absent. Original partial proposal corrected these; completion retains them.

items.finding: The Michigan sentence is accurate and correctly labelled second-hand. Two points for the claim's closing sentences, as far as this source goes: (1) 'none compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people who use the drugs outside treatment' should allow that this review relays, without figures, three studies that compared fatal cases with survivors of overdose (one of them, by its title in the reference list, measured serum morphine in living people who use heroin); suggested: 'none of the studies read here made such a comparison itself'. (2) The review does not say who classified Monforte's deaths or whether the levels were known, so 'the people who decided the cause of death knew the measured levels' is not supported by this source.
items.reason: Full Darke supplied PDF read, including references; p.1767 rendered. Survivor comparisons are relayed without numbers, not absent; Monforte certifiers and access to levels are not stated. 1977 is publication year, not an established study period.

items.finding: Accurate overall, with four wording corrections. (1) 'with no stated selection rules' is not right: the review states broad inclusion rules (publications where cannabis was believed to have contributed to an emergency admission for a cardiovascular event or to the death; epidemiological studies designed to examine a link), searched PubMed and Scopus with listed keywords; what it lacks is search dates, counts and any appraisal, and its tables present a selection of publications. Suggested: with broad inclusion rules, no search dates and no appraisal. (2) The claim's wording that no minimum blood THC level can show cause hardens the review's hedge: it says minimum causal concentrations may not be possible to give because of delays from death to sampling. (3) CARDIA: no association with cardiovascular-disease mortality (not heart disease alone), in adults aged 18-30 followed for more than 25 years. (4) The firm recommendation (at least a contributory cause) is in the abstract; the discussion words the same step tentatively (arguably sufficient; not unreasonable), and the conclusion says such inclusion should be encouraged, so the claim's verb recommend is fair. The editors' closing inference (counting cannabis as a cause on these criteria would rest on THC being present plus the circumstances) matches the review's own criteria on p. 304.
items.reason: All nine Drummer pages and Tables1–3 read/rendered in this same reader405 review. items.finding: None for the figures attributed to Ketola & Kriikku. Two small points. (1) 'Tenfold or larger differences between drugs for most specimens' understates Table 3: every one of the ten specimens spans more than tenfold between drugs (other blood 16-fold up to bile over 2,000-fold). Many per-drug cells, though, rest on 1-3 results. (2) The claim's later summary calls this 'an unappraised compilation dominated by published poisoning cases'. 'Unappraised' is right. 'Dominated by' is an inference the paper does not state or quantify. The authors say some included studies focus on intoxications and that compiled femoral levels usually exceed the Finnish all-cause reference (Table 2 median 3.35 times). About 87% of results come from the literature (1,442 of 10,993 from the lab). 'Weighted toward poisoning cases' would be closer to the source.
